summary.text: Robert Jackson is the Democratic and Working Families Party nominee for re-election to New York State Senate District 31, covering Washington Heights, Inwood, and other northern and west Manhattan neighborhoods. A longtime Washington Heights resident who first became known as a Community School Board president and co-founder of the Campaign for Fiscal Equity school-funding lawsuit, he served on the New York City Council from 2002 to 2013 and was elected to the Senate in 2018. He chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee and is unopposed in the general election.

paragraphs.text: Born in Harlem and raised in Manhattan, one of nine children according to his official biography, which says his family has lived in Washington Heights since 1975. Born December 18, 1950, according to Wikipedia.

Attended New York City public schools, including P.S. 186 in Washington Heights and Benjamin Franklin High School in the Bronx, and graduated from the State University of New York at New Paltz (1975, per Wikipedia).
After college, worked for the New York State Department of Labor and the Public Employees Federation, a labor union; was elected to New York City Community School Board 6 in 1986.

As Community School Board president, launched the Campaign for Fiscal Equity lawsuit (Campaign for Fiscal Equity v. State of New York) arguing that the state's school-funding formula shortchanged New York City students, and walked 150 miles to Albany to draw attention to the case. The state's highest court ruled for the plaintiffs in 2003.

Elected to the New York City Council in 2001 and served from 2002 to 2013 representing the 7th District in Manhattan, including as Education Committee chair and co-chair of the Black, Latino and Asian Caucus; he was term-limited in 2013.
Ran unsuccessfully for Manhattan Borough President in the 2013 Democratic primary, finishing third, and lost Democratic primaries for State Senate District 31 in 2014 and 2016.
Elected a Democratic District Leader in 2015, according to his official biography.
Elected to the State Senate in 2018, defeating incumbent Marisol Alcantara in the Democratic primary; re-elected in 2020, 2022, and 2024.
Chairs the Senate Civil Service and Pensions Committee in the 2025–2026 session and sits on the Education, Health, Higher Education, Housing, Labor, and New York City Education committees.
According to his official biography, he is married and has three daughters.
